Ac.name: Altocumulus
Ac.summary: White or grey patches and rolls in regular waves — a “mackerel sky” — sitting at 2 to 7 km. It rarely produces rain on its own.

As.name: Altostratus
As.summary: A grey sheet across most of the sky at 2 to 7 km, with the sun showing through weakly as if behind ground glass. It often thickens into rain or snow.

Cb.name: Cumulonimbus
Cb.summary: A towering cloud with a hard cauliflower top that spreads into an anvil, reaching from under 2 km to 12 km or higher. It brings heavy showers, lightning, gusts and hail.

Cc.name: Cirrocumulus
Cc.summary: Tiny white ripples or grains in sheets with no shading, very high at 5 to 13 km. It does not produce rain.

Ci.name: Cirrus
Ci.summary: Thin, wispy white streaks of ice crystals, high at 5 to 13 km. No rain from it directly, but cirrus that steadily thickens can mean rain within a day.

Cs.name: Cirrostratus
Cs.summary: A thin milky veil over the whole sky at 5 to 13 km, with a halo ring around the sun or moon. It often comes before rain or snow within a day.

Ct.name: Contrail
Ct.summary: A straight white line left by an aircraft near 8 to 12 km — not a natural cloud. When contrails linger and spread out, the upper air is moist.

Cu.name: Cumulus
Cu.summary: Detached white cotton-wool puffs with flat grey bases, low below 2 km. Fair weather, unless they build tall through the day into showers.

Ns.name: Nimbostratus
Ns.summary: A thick, dark, featureless grey layer that blots out the sun, low to mid level. This is the cloud of steady, prolonged rain or snow.

Sc.name: Stratocumulus
Sc.summary: Lumpy grey and white rolls covering the sky with bright gaps between them, low below 2 km. Mostly dry, with light drizzle at most.

St.name: Stratus
St.summary: A flat, dull grey sheet like fog lifted just off the ground, very low. Grey and gloomy with drizzle at most, and it usually burns off.
